Battle of Plataea. In 479 BC near the city of Plataea in central Greece, a united Greek coalition decisively defeated the Persian general Mardonius. Combined with the concurrent naval Battle of Mycale, Plataea definitively ended Persian attempts to conquer mainland Greece.

The Spartan regent Pausanias commanded the Greek forces, mustering approximately 40,000 hoplites from multiple city-states, primarily Sparta and Athens. Mardonius, commanding the remaining Persian forces after Xerxes had returned to Asia, fielded roughly 60,000 troops.

The opening phase of battle favored the Persians. Persian cavalry and mounted archers broke the initial Greek advance, forcing a strategic retreat. But Pausanias held firm. He rallied the Spartan phalanx and led them in a charge directly at Mardonius's position. The Persian general fell in hand-to-hand combat, struck down in the midst of battle.

With Mardonius dead, the Persian center collapsed entirely. The rout became general. Estimates suggest 43,000 Persian casualties compared to only roughly 1,600 Greek deaths.

The victory liberated Greek cities in Ionia and the Aegean, establishing Greek autonomy and making Greek culture dominant throughout the region for the next two centuries. Pausanias, the Spartan commander whose tactical restraint and personal courage won the day, became legendary. Mardonius's death symbolized the end of Persian conquest ambitions. The Persian Wars themselves, the broader conflict between Greece and Persia that had defined this era, were now conclusively resolved in Greece's favor. Plataea came just one year after the naval triumph at Salamis, forming the climax to a decade of struggle.
